articles.title: Wall Street Rallies After the Midterms: Dow Jumps 1,569 Points in Its Best Day Since April 2025
articles.description: The Dow surged 3.03% to 53,356.12 on Wednesday, November 4, its best day since April 2025, as the S&P 500 rose 1.58% and the Nasdaq gained 1.44% — adding about $1.2 trillion in market value as oil tumbled.
articles.sources: Invezz, ET Now, TradingKey, TheStreet via The Evergreen Edit, November 4-5, 2026
articles.body:
US stocks rallied sharply on Wednesday, November 4, the first trading day after Democrats were projected to win control of both the House and the Senate, with investors welcoming greater political clarity and a steep drop in oil prices, reports said.

The closing numbers

The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 3.03 percent, or 1,569.40 points, to close at 53,356.12. The S&P 500 rose 1.58 percent to 7,688.62, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.44 percent to 25,736.51, and the small-company Russell 2000 rose 1.58 percent to 2,856.95. ABC News reported it was the Dow’s best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, the day President Trump suspended his reciprocal tariffs, and one roundup called it the biggest post-midterm-election rally in 44 years. The rally added approximately $1.2 trillion to the market capitalisation of US stocks, according to ET Now. All five major US indices closed higher, with the Nasdaq 100 posting the smallest gain as technology lagged the broader advance.

What drove the rally

Hyperscale cloud providers led the gains: Microsoft rose 6.68 percent, Amazon gained 6.12 percent and Apple climbed about 5.31 percent, while Alphabet added 3.18 percent and Meta rose 1.44 percent, according to TradingKey. The rebound followed an overnight plunge — Nasdaq-100 futures had fallen as much as 2.4 percent while counting was under way — before recovering as President Trump said he would accept the results. Falling oil prices, lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar also supported the broad rally: Brent crude plunged about 9 percent to around $94.61 a barrel and US crude fell to about $88.05, as signs of diplomacy over the Iran war gave markets hope of a settlement. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.9 percent after topping 5.3 percent a day earlier.

The split underneath

Not everything rallied. Nvidia fell 3.17 percent, Micron dropped 7.00 percent, Broadcom slipped 2.00 percent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.13 percent, as memory-chip shares were sold off after hours — Qualcomm slumped nearly 6 percent after its earnings miss. SpaceX fell 3.81 percent and Tesla dropped 3.34 percent. Analysts urged caution, noting that futures can reverse quickly and that gridlock — a Democratic Congress facing a Republican president with veto power — remains the most likely policy outcome. Investors now await Friday’s October jobs report and next week’s inflation data, which will test whether the post-election rally has staying power or was a one-day relief trade.

articles.title: October Jobs Report Due Friday: Economists Expect About 65,000 New Jobs as the Fed Watches
articles.description: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October jobs report on Friday, November 6, at 8:30 a.m. ET, with economists expecting roughly 50,000-65,000 new jobs and unemployment holding at 4.2% after September's weak 29,000.
articles.sources: E8 Markets, AInvest, Continuum Economics, ByDFi, November 1-5, 2026
articles.body:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October Employment Situation report on Friday, November 6, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time, in what could be the most consequential economic data point before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, previews published this week said.

What economists expect

Economists expect October payroll growth of roughly 65,000, more than double September’s gain, while the unemployment rate is expected to remain near 4.2 percent, according to previews. Forecasts are spread out: Pantheon expects 100,000, citing firmer small-business and regional Fed surveys, while Continuum Economics forecasts a more subdued 50,000, with private-sector payrolls up 45,000. FinancialJuice cites a consensus of 65,000, while other previews put the range at 35,000 to 125,000. On wages, forecasters look for average hourly earnings to rise about 0.3 percent on the month, though Continuum expects 0.2 percent, which would see year-over-year wage growth fall to 2.8 percent from 3.0 percent — the slowest since May 2021.

The weak September baseline

September payroll employment increased by just 29,000, far short of the roughly 90,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate held at 4.2 percent. The same release cut a combined 60,000 jobs from the two prior months: July was revised from a gain of 21,000 to a loss of 10,000, and August was cut from 162,000 to 133,000. Yet the labour market is not cracking in the usual way: weekly initial jobless claims came in at 194,000 in late October, near the lowest levels since 1969 and below 200,000 for seven straight weeks. Bloomberg Economics summed up the dynamic as a “low-hire, low-fire” market that is “losing momentum, but not breaking.” The paradox is striking: the US economy grew at a 3.4 percent annualised pace in the third quarter, up from 2.2 percent in the second, while September produced only 29,000 net new jobs. Productivity has grown at a 2.5 percent annualised pace since early 2023, the fastest sustained run in decades, which helps explain how output can surge while hiring stays thin.

Why the Fed cares

The report matters mainly through the December Fed decision. At its October 28 meeting the Fed held rates at 3.75 to 4.00 percent on a 10-2 vote, with two dissents actually wanting to hike further, and markets were pricing about a 78 percent chance of a December hike as of November 4. A strong jobs report would tend to raise that probability, and a weak one to lower it. But economists caution against over-reading a single month: the payroll number is published as an estimate and revised in the two releases that follow, and with the breakeven hiring rate now close to zero — KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk puts it near zero, inside the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 100,000 — even a month of 45,000 jobs is enough to hold unemployment steady. Unemployment has stayed below 4.5 percent for 59 straight months through September, the longest such stretch since World War II. Sector detail will also matter: Continuum expects education and health services to add roughly 25,000 jobs, while finance and information are each projected to lose 10,000, with finance having already shed 129,000 jobs since May 2025 — weakness one forecaster links to the rapid integration of AI and automation.

articles.title: US Futures Plunge, Then Rebound, as Democrats Sweep Congress
articles.description: US stock futures fell sharply overnight as Democrats won both chambers — Nasdaq-100 futures down as much as 2.4% — then recovered most of the drop by Wednesday morning as Trump said he would accept the results.
articles.sources: Reuters via Gulf News, Economic Times, Invezz, Eastern Herald, November 4, 2026
articles.body:
US stock futures lurched lower, then recovered, on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, with the early sell-off led by AI and technology stocks and the rebound helped by President Donald Trump saying he would accept the results, reports said.

The overnight drop

Nasdaq-100 futures fell as much as 2.4 percent and S&P 500 futures as much as 1.4 percent while counting was under way, as investors weighed the prospect of tighter rules on data centres and AI, possibly higher taxes on companies, and fights over the budget and the debt ceiling. The dollar weakened to a more than one-month low, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.9 percent after topping 5.3 percent a day earlier, a 24-year high.

The rebound

By Wednesday morning the losses had largely been erased: Dow futures were up about 789 points, or 1.5 percent, S&P 500 futures up about 1.1 percent and Nasdaq futures up about 1 percent in later readings, helped by AMD and Arista earnings and by Trump's conciliatory comments. Analysts urged caution, noting that futures can reverse quickly and that gridlock — a Democratic Congress facing a Republican president with veto power — remains the most likely policy outcome. Investors now await Friday's October jobs report and next week's inflation data.

articles.title: Wall Street on Election Eve: Dow Slips, S&P and Nasdaq Gain Ahead of Results
articles.description: On Tuesday, the Dow fell 197 points to 51,786.72 while the S&P 500 gained 0.36% to 7,568.92 and the Nasdaq rose 0.83% to 25,372.01, as investors positioned for the midterm results and digested Apple and Palantir earnings.
articles.sources: Wall Street Journal figures via Eastern Herald, Reuters, November 4, 2026
articles.body:
Wall Street closed mixed on Tuesday, November 3, as investors positioned for the midterm election results and digested a heavy earnings slate, with the Dow slipping while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained, reports said.

The closing numbers

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 197.26 points, or 0.38 percent, to 51,786.72. The S&P 500 gained 27.52 points, or 0.36 percent, to 7,568.92, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 207.65 points, or 0.83 percent, to 25,372.01, according to the Wall Street Journal figures cited in coverage. The session came a day after the Nasdaq-100 closed more than 10 percent below its all-time closing high, confirming a correction in the tech-heavy index.

What drove the split

Apple and Palantir shares slid despite better-than-expected results, on margin and valuation worries, while AMD and Arista rallied after the bell on strong AI-linked results. After the close, futures weakened as projections showed Democrats winning both chambers, before recovering on Wednesday. The week ahead still holds the October jobs report on Friday and September's JOLTS job-openings data, which investors will watch for the economy's direction under a newly divided government.

articles.title: Wall Street Mixed on Election Day as Nasdaq Sits in Correction and Oil Swings
articles.description: US stock futures were mixed on Tuesday as investors awaited midterm results, with the Nasdaq-100 in correction after closing more than 10% below its high, while Apple and Palantir fell after earnings.
articles.sources: Reuters via Kitco and Business Times, Bloomberg via Swissinfo, TipRanks, November 3, 2026
articles.body:
US stock futures traded mixed ahead of Tuesday's market open as investors weighed corporate earnings and awaited the midterm elections, with Apple and Palantir shares sliding despite better-than-expected results, Reuters and TipRanks reported on November 3.

A correction in tech

The Nasdaq-100 closed more than 10 percent below its all-time closing high on Monday, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction, as investors grow wary of Big Tech's soaring AI spending and little evidence of adequate returns. On Monday the Nasdaq fell 1.07 percent and the S&P 500 declined 0.51 percent, while the Dow gained 0.41 percent. On Tuesday morning, Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 0.3 to 0.7 percent, S&P 500 futures were roughly flat to slightly lower, and Dow futures were down about 0.3 to 0.9 percent in early readings that moved through the morning.

Oil, earnings and the week ahead

Apple fell about 3.8 to 4.4 percent in premarket trading after warning memory-chip costs would pressure its holiday-quarter margin, and Palantir slid about 4.6 percent in early trading despite raising guidance. Oil swung through the session: Brent crude fell below $102 a barrel at one point on an unconfirmed report about a draft memorandum from Qatari mediators on Iran, then rose again after reports of a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island, with Brent around $105.78 and WTI around $97.50. Investors also awaited September's JOLTS job-openings report and Friday's jobs report, plus AMD earnings after Tuesday's bell.

articles.title: Pfizer Raises 2026 Forecast After Third-Quarter Beat Led by Eliquis and Cancer Drugs
articles.description: Pfizer raised its full-year revenue outlook to $62-64 billion and adjusted earnings to $2.95-3.05 per share after third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion beat estimates, helped by Eliquis and Padcev.
articles.sources: Bloomberg via The Edge Singapore, Dow Jones via Morningstar, Reuters via Devdiscourse, November 3, 2026
articles.body:
Pfizer raised its 2026 forecast on Tuesday, November 3, after third-quarter results beat Wall Street expectations, as growing demand for newer medicines helped offset declining sales of its Covid-19 products, Bloomberg and Dow Jones reported.

The quarter in numbers

Third-quarter revenue was $16.58 billion, little changed from $16.65 billion a year earlier but above the roughly $15.87 billion analysts expected. Adjusted earnings were $0.87 per share, ahead of the $0.73 to $0.74 analysts expected, while reported net income fell 8 percent to $3.24 billion. Sales of blood thinner Eliquis rose 25 percent to $2.52 billion, and the company pointed to strong demand for recently acquired cancer drug Padcev. Revenue excluding Comirnaty and Paxlovid grew 7 percent on an operational basis.

The raised outlook — and a new CFO

Pfizer now expects full-year revenue of $62 billion to $64 billion, up from $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion, and adjusted earnings of $2.95 to $3.05 per share, up from $2.80 to $3.00. The outlook includes a $650 million licensing-related acquired research charge, worth about $0.10 per share. Separately, Pfizer named Cecile Guegan as permanent chief financial officer, effective November 1, after she served as interim CFO since August.

articles.title: Berkshire Hathaway Enters Earnings Week Under Scrutiny as GEICO Weakens
articles.description: Berkshire Hathaway heads into its third-quarter earnings release with analysts expecting about $97.3 billion in revenue but lower per-share profit, as GEICO underwriting softens and industrial cash flow stays strong.
articles.sources: Ad-hoc News / Yahoo Finance via Zacks, Seeking Alpha, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
Berkshire Hathaway enters its third-quarter 2026 earnings week with analysts expecting revenue growth but a lower per-share result than a year earlier, according to previews published on November 2.

What analysts expect

A Yahoo Finance preview cited by reports put the Zacks consensus at $97.3 billion in revenue, up 2.5 percent year over year, and $5.91 per Class B share, down 5.6 percent. The consensus had moved 4.4 percent higher over the previous 30 days, though Zacks' most accurate estimate of $5.87 sat below consensus, and its model did not conclusively signal a beat. Zacks noted Berkshire had beaten consensus in three of its previous four quarters, with an average surprise of 12.04 percent.

Insurance versus industrials

Insurance operations are expected to benefit from pricing, retention and higher average auto premiums, potentially offsetting softer GEICO results: GEICO's pre-tax underwriting earnings fell about 40 percent in the first half of 2026 as claims severity and expenses rose, and its combined ratio worsened to 91.2 percent from 83.5 percent. Offsetting that, manufacturing, service, retailing, BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy generated roughly $6.9 billion after tax in the first half, nearly 20 percent higher year over year, with $21.7 billion of operating cash flow.

articles.title: Wall Street Futures Rebound After a Brutal October for Tech Stocks
articles.description: US stock futures rose on Monday after Friday's selloff wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value, capping the Nasdaq's worst month since April 2025 — with Apple earnings and Friday's jobs report ahead.
articles.sources: CNBC TV18 via TradingView, Business Recorder, JorgAI, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
US stock futures started the week higher on Monday after Friday's brutal selloff, with Dow futures up more than 165 points and S&P 500 futures up about 30 points, CNBC TV18 reported via TradingView on November 2.

October's damage

The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost almost 7 percent in October, its worst month since the April 2025 tariff rout, as worries about negative cash flow and the sheer scale of AI capital spending pushed up the cost of insuring corporate defaults. Global markets steadied in Asia on Monday as investors hoped Apple earnings later in the day would offer relief from AI cash-burn worries, while oil prices eased after talks continued between Iranian and Qatari mediators.

A packed week ahead

Beyond Apple and Palantir on Monday night, the week brings AMD on Tuesday night, Qualcomm, Arm and Uber on Wednesday, and the October jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday, November 6 — alongside the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, which polls suggest could deliver a Democratic sweep of Congress. S&P 500 futures edged up 0.4 percent and Nasdaq futures bounced 0.8 percent in early trading, according to Business Recorder's market roundup.

articles.title: S&P Downgrades Meta's Credit Outlook to Negative After $95 Billion AI Debt Plan
articles.description: S&P Global Ratings changed Meta Platforms' credit outlook from stable to negative on October 31, days after the company said it would raise $95 billion to build AI data centers.
articles.sources: Financial News, October 31-November 1, 2026
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings downgraded the credit outlook for Meta Platforms from stable to negative on October 31, Financial News reported, adding a new worry for investors already rattled by the cost of the artificial intelligence buildout.

The debt behind the downgrade

Meta had announced on October 26 that it would raise $95 billion to build infrastructure such as AI data centers. The scale of that borrowing, coming alongside a surge in capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion and $145 billion for 2026, prompted the ratings agency to take a more cautious view of the company's credit profile. Meta's shares had already fallen 7% on October 22 when the spending guidance was announced, and its free cash flow turned negative even as the company beat revenue estimates.

A wider reckoning on AI spending

The outlook change lands in a week when the AI trade came under heavy pressure: Alphabet reported negative quarterly free cash flow, Amazon reported a $42.4 billion free-cash-flow shortfall over 12 months, and Intel plunged 29% on weak guidance. An outlook downgrade is not a rating cut — it signals that a cut is more likely if trends continue — but it underscores how the market's question has shifted from how fast companies can build AI capacity to how they will pay for it.

articles.title: Week Ahead: Apple, Palantir and AMD Earnings Plus Jobs Report Test an AI-Wary Market
articles.description: Apple and Palantir report on Monday, AMD and Super Micro follow on Tuesday, and the October jobs report lands on Friday — a week that will test whether the AI selloff continues after October's rout.
articles.sources: Reuters via Economic Times, TradingView/Stocktwits, November 1, 2026
articles.body:
US markets head into another busy week, with corporate earnings, key economic data and the midterm elections all set to test investors after a bruising October, Reuters reported on October 31.

The earnings calendar

Apple and Palantir are set to report on Monday after the closing bell, followed by Advanced Micro Devices and Super Micro Computer on Tuesday. Apple is expected to report earnings per share of $1.98 on revenue of $113.27 billion, Palantir $0.41 per share on $2.18 billion, and AMD $1.94 per share on $13.1 billion in revenue. Investors will watch not just the headline numbers but what the companies say about demand and the outlook for AI-related spending, after disappointing results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel drove the Nasdaq to its worst month since March 2025.

Jobs data and the election

The week ends with the October jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday, giving investors a fresh read on the labor market after a relatively weak September reading; economists expect roughly 55,000 jobs added, according to a Dow Jones estimate cited by MarketWatch. In between, voters decide the midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, an outcome that could shape the outlook for AI regulation. With over half of the S&P 500 having reported third-quarter results, overall earnings are on pace to rise 31.6% for the period, according to LSEG data — a reminder that the selloff is about spending and returns, not a collapse in profits.

articles.title: October Ends in the Red for Tech: Nasdaq Down 5.3% for the Month as Investors Rotate to Defensives
articles.description: The Nasdaq dropped 5.3% in October, its steepest monthly decline since March 2025, while the Dow gained 1.7% as investors rotated into defensive stocks at month-end.
articles.sources: Reuters via Business Times, Dimsum Daily, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
US stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, October 30, ending a volatile month in which the artificial intelligence trade — the market's main engine for much of the year — went into reverse, Reuters reported on October 31.

How the month closed

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31, the S&P 500 lost 1.82% to 7,580.07, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00. For the month, the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its steepest decline since March 2025, the S&P 500 slipped 0.9%, while the Dow gained 1.7%. The S&P 500 technology sector posted its largest monthly percentage loss since March 2025, and communication services registered its biggest monthly drop since April 2022.

Friday's trading turned more disorderly in the afternoon as investors trimmed positions ahead of next week's midterm elections. Defensive names helped limit losses on the blue-chip index: Walmart and Coca-Cola each rose more than 1%, while Merck and Amgen also advanced. CoreWeave shares slumped 37% in October and Nebius nearly 35% as funding costs rose.

Earnings season, in context

Third-quarter earnings season has passed the halfway mark, with 299 S&P 500 companies having reported and 82% beating consensus expectations, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. Analysts now expect third-quarter earnings growth of 31.6% year on year. The tension for markets is not whether companies are profitable, but whether enormous AI infrastructure spending turns into cash quickly enough — the question that drove October's selloff, and the one investors will carry into November, when Apple reports earnings on November 2.

articles.title: Exxon and Chevron Beat Profit Forecasts as a $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Hits Crypto Stocks
articles.description: Oil supermajors Exxon Mobil and Chevron both beat quarterly profit expectations, while Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood fell 7.2% to 10.6% after hackers reportedly stole $6.3 billion from Binance.
articles.sources: Reuters via Business Times, Bilyonaryo, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
Oil supermajors Exxon Mobil and Chevron both beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from soaring profit margins as energy supply disruptions arising from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine lifted refining economics, Reuters reported on October 31.

Energy leads a down day

Energy was one of the few bright spots on Friday's down session, with six of the 11 S&P 500 sectors rising, led by Energy at 1.91%. The strength contrasted with the broader market, where the S&P 500 fell 1.82% and the Nasdaq 2.86%. Oil prices rose about 2% on the day, adding to concern about the health of a US economy that many investors see as dependent on the AI buildout for its momentum.

Crypto stocks slide after the Binance hack

Cryptocurrency-related firms fell after reports that hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange. Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood dropped between 7.2% and 10.6%, and Bitcoin fell about 3%. The episode is a reminder of how quickly exchange security news can spill into listed crypto stocks, even on a day when the dominant market story is AI spending rather than digital assets.

articles.title: Stocks Fall Thursday as Alphabet's Worst Day Ever Drags the Nasdaq Down 1.4%
articles.description: The Dow fell 0.3% to 52,342.56, the S&P 500 slipped 0.3% to 7,720.39 and the Nasdaq dropped 1.4% on Thursday, as Alphabet plunged 12.6% in its worst single-day performance since trading began.
articles.sources: Zacks, FinancialAdvsr, Economic Times, October 29-30, 2026
articles.body:
US stock markets closed lower on Thursday, October 29, ending a three-day winning run, as disappointing earnings and guidance from AI-powered corporate giants dented confidence in risky assets and an elevated inflation reading hurt sentiment.

How the benchmarks performed

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%, or 132.54 points, to close at 52,342.56, though 23 of its 30 components ended in positive territory. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended at 26,184.72, sliding 1.4%, or 365.13 points, on weak performance by AI leaders. The S&P 500 shed 0.3% to finish at 7,720.39, even as nine of its 11 sectors closed higher, led by health care and real estate. The fear gauge, the CBOE Volatility Index, rose 1.7% to 17.20.

The Russell 2000 bucked the trend, gaining 1.01% to 2,859.22, and four in five S&P 500 stocks rose — a sign the damage was concentrated in the biggest technology names rather than the broader market.

Alphabet leads the slide

Alphabet's Class A shares dropped 12.6% in their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago, after third-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings missed expectations and raised concerns about cash depletion from AI investment. Fortinet fell 20.1% and ServiceNow 27% after their own results, with ServiceNow also suffering its worst single-day performance on record, according to Zacks.

Economic data added to the gloom: initial jobless claims decreased by 1,000 to 194,000 for the week ended October 24, below expectations, but September inflation data released alongside the GDP report kept the focus on price pressures. Treasury yields eased after the Fed and European Central Bank holds, with the 10-year yield closing at 4.98%, down 7 basis points.

What Friday brought

The selling did not stop at Thursday's close. Amazon and Intel reported after the bell, and Nasdaq futures fell more than 2% on Friday morning as their results deepened concerns over AI spending. Despite Friday's decline, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq remained on course for weekly gains, though the Nasdaq was headed for its first monthly decline in three months.

articles.title: US Labor Costs Rose 0.8% in Q3 as Wage Growth Slowed, Easing — but Not Erasing — Inflation Fears
articles.description: The Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, down from 0.9% in the second, with wages up 0.7% — a modest slowdown that suggests the labor market is unlikely to be a major inflation risk, Reuters reports.
articles.sources: Reuters, BLS Employment Cost Index, October 30, 2026
articles.body:
US labor costs increased moderately in the third quarter, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday, October 30, offering the Federal Reserve some relief on wage-driven inflation even as broader price pressures remain elevated.

What the numbers show

The Employment Cost Index, the broadest measure of labor costs, rose 0.8% last quarter after increasing 0.9% in the April-June period, Reuters reported. Labor costs advanced 3.4% in the 12 months through September, unchanged from the year through June. Wages and salaries, which account for the bulk of labor costs, climbed 0.7% last quarter after rising 0.9% in the second quarter, and increased 3.1% over the year, down from 3.2%.

Private-sector wages rose 0.8% in the quarter and 3.1% over the year, while public-sector wages climbed 0.6% and 3.2% respectively. The ECI is closely watched by policymakers because it adjusts for shifts in job mix and quality, giving a cleaner read on underlying pay pressure than average hourly earnings.

Why it matters for the Fed

“Labor-cost inflation continues to move in the right direction,” Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets, told Reuters, adding that while consumer inflation remains elevated, the Fed will take some comfort that the labor market is no longer a significant source of price pressures.

The relief is partial. Wages adjusted for inflation dropped 0.6% in the 12 months through September, after declining 0.3% in the year through June — meaning pay is still lagging prices for workers. And with September PCE inflation at 3.6% year on year and core PCE at 3.1%, markets still price about a 75% chance of a December rate hike, according to CME data cited in Friday previews. The ECI was the last major data point of October ahead of the Fed's December 8-9 meeting.

articles.title: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%–4% in 10–2 Vote as Warsh Says Politics Played No Role
articles.description: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate steady on October 28 in a 10-2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favor of another hike as inflation stays above target.
articles.sources: USA TODAY, TRT World, Reuters, October 28-29, 2026
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on October 28, leaving its benchmark federal funds rate unchanged at a range of 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, days before the midterm elections and one month after its first rate hike in three years.

A divided committee

Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring another quarter-point increase. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in the decision, telling reporters he had heard no reference to politics or elections during two days of deliberations. The Fed's statement said accumulating more information would help determine the policy stance needed to return inflation to its 2% target.

Inflation still above target

Consumer price inflation was running at about 3.7% in the year to September, roughly a point above the Fed's goal, with limited progress in recent months. Officials described economic growth as strong and job gains as keeping pace with workforce growth, but expressed concern that stronger-than-expected inflation could become entrenched as businesses and households adjust their expectations.

What to watch next

Traders raised their bets on a December hike after the decision, with CME FedWatch pricing roughly 85% odds of another quarter-point increase at the Fed's final meeting of the year. Warsh also announced a structural change: from 2027, one of the Fed's eight annual meetings will be devoted entirely to broad monetary policy strategy, with no rate vote, rising to two such sessions in 2028.

articles.title: US Economy Grew 3.4% in Q3, Fastest in a Year, Beating Forecasts
articles.description: US GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, beating forecasts as consumer spending and AI-driven investment powered the strongest expansion in a year.
articles.sources: US Bureau of Economic Analysis, USA TODAY, KPMG, October 29, 2026
articles.body:
The US economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter and beating economist forecasts, according to the Commerce Department's advance estimate released October 29.

What drove the acceleration

The expansion primarily reflected faster investment and an upturn in government spending, partly offset by a decline in exports and rising imports. Consumer spending grew at a robust 3.8% pace, matching the second quarter for the strongest back-to-back gains since the pandemic rebound, with services including healthcare leading the way. Equipment spending surged at a 20.9% annual rate, its third straight quarter of double-digit gains, riding the AI investment boom.

Inflation data released alongside

The September personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.6% from a year earlier, slightly below forecasts, while core PCE rose 3.1%. Within the quarter, the core PCE index came in at 2.5%, down from 3.3% in the second quarter. Personal income rose only 0.2% in September and the saving rate fell to 3.8%, its lowest since October 2022, a reminder that household buffers are thinning even as spending holds up.

Why it matters for the Fed

The day before the release, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had described activity as expanding at a strong pace with resilient domestic spending and robust capital investment. The stronger growth reading, landing a day after the Fed held rates steady, keeps the December decision finely balanced: solid growth argues against urgency, while inflation still well above 2% keeps another hike firmly on the table.

articles.title: Wall Street Rallies for Second Day as AI Stocks Lead Ahead of Fed Decision
articles.description: US stocks rose for a second straight session, with the Nasdaq jumping 1.18% to 26,477.81 as chipmakers rallied ahead of the Federal Reserve's rate decision.
articles.sources: Zacks, Malay Mail/AFP, Newspim, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
US stock markets closed higher on Tuesday, buoyed by a rejuvenated artificial intelligence trade, strong economic data and declining crude oil prices. All three major indexes ended in positive territory for a second straight session.

The numbers

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 16 points to close at 52,377.57 after a choppy session that saw it down nearly 130 points at its intraday low. The S&P 500 gained 0.6% to finish at 7,722.60, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.18%, or 308.43 points, to 26,477.81. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 3.6% after Broadcom's $63 billion financing deal tied to Anthropic, and the CBOE Volatility Index fell 4.7% to 17.52. A total of 16.1 billion shares changed hands, below the recent 20-session average.

"The buy-the-dip trade is taking place," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare. "You have the market being led by the AI stocks and particularly the semiconductors and those larger hyperscaler names." Nvidia rose 0.91%, while AMD gained 5.45% and Broadcom 4.00%.

Not everything rallied: six of the 11 S&P sectors closed lower, a reminder that the advance was carried by a powerful technology pocket rather than broad participation. The next test arrives Wednesday, when the Federal Reserve announces its rate decision and Alphabet and Microsoft report earnings after the bell.

articles.title: Fed Decision Day: Markets Price a Hold as Warsh Faces First Big Test
articles.description: The Federal Reserve announces its rate decision at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday, with markets pricing about a 90% chance of a hold at 3.75% to 4.00%.
articles.sources: Investopedia, Financial Adviser markets briefing, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
The Federal Reserve announces its interest rate decision at 2:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday, with Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference set for 2:30 p.m. Markets are widely expecting a hold, pricing roughly a 90% chance that the target range stays at 3.75% to 4.00% after September's 25-basis-point hike, the first in three years.

What to watch

The statement and press conference will be read for signals about a possible December move. Associated Press reporting named Beth Hammack and Lorie Logan as possible dissenters favouring a hike, which would be a notable split if it materialises. The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.99%, down a basis point on the day, with the 2-year at 4.70%.

The decision lands in the middle of a crowded earnings day: Alphabet and Microsoft headline 46 S&P 500 companies reporting, and futures were mixed ahead of the open, with the Dow down 0.2% and the Nasdaq up 0.4% in early trading. For investors, the question is less whether the Fed holds, and more what Warsh says about what comes next.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO Filing Lifts Stocks as Wall Street Rallies
articles.description: US stocks rose Monday after Anthropic filed to go public, with the S&P 500 closing up 0.7 percent and the Nasdaq gaining 0.8 percent ahead of the Fed's decision.
articles.sources: Reuters via Kitco, Zacks, Saxo
articles.body:
US stocks rose on Monday after Anthropic filed to go public on the Nasdaq, reviving appetite for artificial intelligence names and breaking a run of back-to-back weekly losses for the major indexes. The S&P 500 closed at 7,676.77, up 0.70 percent, while the Nasdaq Composite ended at 26,169.38, up 0.8 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3 percent to 52,361.58, according to Zacks and Saxo market summaries.

The filing was reported to disclose $16.29 billion of revenue for the six months to June, a figure that gave investors a fresh datapoint on the scale of the AI industry's leading private companies. The listing would be another major technology IPO of 2026, following SpaceX's blockbuster debut in June, according to CNBC TV18's market coverage.

Tech shares lead the way

Gains were led by large technology names, though the move was uneven. Tesla gained 5.21 percent, Nvidia rose 2.39 percent and Microsoft added 1.54 percent, while Meta fell 1.88 percent, Apple slipped 1.10 percent and Alphabet declined 1.06 percent, according to Saxo's session summary. Nine of the 11 S&P 500 sectors ended in positive territory, with information technology, industrials and consumer discretionary leading the advance.

The CBOE Volatility Index, Wall Street's fear gauge, fell 5.5 percent to 18.39, and advancers outnumbered decliners on both the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq. A retreat in crude oil also eased pressure on stocks, with Brent crude slipping for a second straight day and US West Texas Intermediate futures shedding nearly 1 percent to around $101 per barrel.

Fed decision and big earnings ahead

Investors now turn to a busy week. The Federal Reserve's policy decision is due Wednesday, with markets widely expecting rates to be held steady, and several of the largest technology companies are due to report earnings later in the week. Their results will be parsed for signs of whether hefty AI investments are translating into growth, a question that has driven much of this year's market debate.

On Tuesday morning, US stock index futures ticked higher as crude prices extended their decline, with Dow E-minis up 169 points, S&P 500 E-minis up 15 points and Nasdaq 100 E-minis up 79 points in early trading, according to Reuters. Coca-Cola shares inched up in premarket trading after the beverage giant raised its annual profit forecast, while PayPal fell close to 1 percent despite lifting its annual adjusted profit view.

articles.title: Broadcom's $63 Billion Financing Powers Anthropic Technology Deal
articles.description: A group of banks and Blackstone announced $63 billion in financing for the purchase of Broadcom technology for Anthropic, lifting chip stocks across the board.
articles.sources: CNBC TV18, Reuters
articles.body:
Chip stocks got a lift on Tuesday after a group of banks, including Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley, along with Blackstone, announced $63 billion in financing for the purchase of Broadcom technology for Anthropic, according to CNBC TV18's market coverage. The deal underscores how deeply the AI boom now reaches into financing, with lenders and private capital backing the infrastructure behind frontier AI models.

Broadcom shares rose more than 2 percent on the news, and sentiment spread across chipmakers, with Micron Technology up more than 2 percent, Advanced Micro Devices gaining nearly 2 percent and Nvidia rising around 1 percent in early trading. The gains built on the previous session's rally, when major averages ended higher after Anthropic filed to go public on the Nasdaq.

Why the financing matters

Financing packages of this size show how capital-intensive the AI buildout has become. Training and running advanced models requires vast amounts of specialized chips, networking equipment and data-center capacity, and the companies building that infrastructure increasingly rely on large-scale debt and private financing alongside equity. The involvement of major banks and Blackstone signals that mainstream finance now treats AI infrastructure as a core lending market rather than a speculative bet.

For Broadcom, the deal ties its technology directly to one of the AI industry's most prominent model developers. For Anthropic, access to Broadcom technology at this scale supports its push to expand the computing capacity behind its models as it prepares for public markets.

Part of a broader chip rally

The financing news arrived as investors weighed a packed week of catalysts, including the Federal Reserve's policy decision on Wednesday and earnings from several of the largest technology companies. Chip stocks have been among the market's most sensitive barometers of AI sentiment all year, rising on signs of strong demand and falling when investors question whether spending will pay off.

Analysts will be watching whether the financing translates into sustained orders and revenue for suppliers, and whether Anthropic's public listing, once completed, gives the market a new benchmark for valuing private AI companies. For now, the deal has added fresh momentum to a sector that has driven much of Wall Street's gains this year.

articles.title: Wall Street Heads Into Fed Week as Oil Near $117 and Stocks Slip
articles.description: Stocks slipped Friday as Brent crude settled at $116.72 and the 10-year yield closed at 5 percent, setting up a pivotal week with a Fed decision and big tech earnings.
articles.sources: Zacks, Reuters, FinancialAdvsr, TipRanks
articles.body:
U.S. stocks slipped on Friday as oil stayed elevated and bond yields climbed, setting up a pivotal week that brings a Federal Reserve decision, major economic data and earnings from three of the world's largest technology companies.

The S and P 500 fell 0.52 percent to 7,623.68 on Friday, its second straight weekly decline, as oil's rally and inflation worries weighed on shares. The Dow dropped 1.23 percent, or 652.82 points, to 52,215.16, though it still finished the week higher. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.21 percent to 25,955.34, and the Russell 2000 eased 0.29 percent.

Oil replaces AI as the market's main worry

Brent crude settled at $116.72 a barrel on Friday after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia pushed prices higher. Energy was the only clear sector gainer, with Exxon, Chevron and ConocoPhillips all closing at record highs, while eight of the eleven S and P sectors ended in negative territory. The Energy Select Sector fund advanced 2.6 percent, while consumer staples tumbled 1.9 percent.

Oil fell in early Asian trade on Monday after reports that Qatari mediators were in Tehran over the weekend, and that President Trump had ruled out an immediate strike on Iran. The ten-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 5.00 percent, a level that keeps borrowing costs high across the economy.

Fed expected to hold on Wednesday

The Federal Open Market Committee meets October 27 and 28, with the decision due Wednesday at 2 p.m. Eastern, followed by a press conference with Chair Kevin Warsh. The target range is 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent, after the Fed raised rates 25 basis points in September, its first hike since 2023.

Market pricing as of October 20 showed about 83 percent odds of a pause and 17 percent odds of a quarter-point hike. Traders will also focus on the ADP employment report and durable goods orders on Tuesday, and the personal consumption expenditures inflation reading and weekly jobless claims on Thursday, alongside third-quarter growth figures.

Big tech earnings take center stage

The earnings calendar is heavy. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are among the key names reporting this week, alongside Boeing, SoFi, PayPal, Robinhood, Visa, Intel, Mastercard, Starbucks, Exxon Mobil and Chevron.

Investors are focused on AI spending and profitability after a bruising week for technology shares, and on whether the big spenders can show returns on their massive infrastructure investments. U.S. stock futures were largely steady on Monday morning as oil retreated, with Tesla gaining in premarket trading after Barclays upgraded the stock to overweight from equal-weight.

The fear gauge, the CBOE Volatility Index, rose 2.2 percent to 19.45 on Friday, and decliners outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. With the Fed, inflation data and the biggest earnings reports of the season all landing in four sessions, volatility is likely to stay elevated.

articles.title: Trend Hedge Funds Suffer Worst Week Since 2024 as AI Stocks Slide, Goldman Says
articles.description: Trend-following hedge funds just had their worst week in two years, Goldman Sachs told clients, as concern about the payoff from heavy AI spending ignited volatility across stocks and bonds.
articles.sources: Reuters, Goldman Sachs prime brokerage note
articles.body:
Trend-following hedge funds suffered their worst weekly performance in two years last week, as concern about the eventual payoff from hefty AI spending ignited volatility across stocks and bonds, according to a Goldman Sachs note seen by Reuters on Monday.

Systematic long-short hedge funds, whose algorithms ride market trends until they peter out, fell 2 percent on the week, their worst showing since 2024. Fundamental long-short strategies drew down another 1.1 percent. Single stocks collectively saw the largest pulling back of positions since late July, and U.S. equities have been net sold for a third straight week, and in four of the last five weeks.

Tech led the slide

The Nasdaq 100, home to the world's largest technology stocks, fell 5.5 percent last week, its biggest weekly fall since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs roiled world markets. Last week's fall was led in part by a 10 percent weekly slide in shares of Meta, which reported strong earnings but indicated it would need to raise more capital for its AI investments, sending shivers through markets.

Goldman said its prime brokerage desk reported $20 billion in selling of technology stocks over the last two weeks, close to July's major unwind, which saw $23 billion in selling.

Bonds whipsawed too

Bond markets were also volatile, as investors sought the relative safety of U.S. Treasuries while selling the debt of more fragile economies, such as France. The combination of falling stocks and jumping bond yields is exactly the environment that punishes trend-following strategies, which are built to profit from steady, persistent moves rather than sudden reversals.

The damage has not erased the year for these funds. Fundamental long-short strategies are down 3.8 percent for the month so far but still up 8.8 percent this year, while systematic strategies are down 1.1 percent so far in October but up 18.7 percent so far this year, according to the note.

What it signals

The episode is a reminder that the AI trade, for all its momentum, can reverse violently when investors start questioning the returns. Heavy spending announcements that once lifted shares are now being read as warnings about cash burn, and funds that loaded up on the trend are being forced to unwind in a hurry.

Whether the selling marks a lasting rotation or a brief shakeout will depend heavily on this week's earnings from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, and on Wednesday's Federal Reserve decision. For now, the message from Goldman's data is clear: the smart money spent last week heading for the exits, not adding to the trade.

articles.title: Meta Lifts 2026 AI Spending Toward $145 Billion and Adds a Nonvoting Stock Class
articles.description: Meta narrowed its 2026 capital spending outlook to $135–145 billion and unveiled nonvoting Class C shares to fund its AI push — then watched its stock fall more than 7%.
articles.sources: Business Times, Channel NewsAsia, Crypto Briefing, Meta Q3 2026 results
articles.body:
Meta Platforms boosted its capital spending outlook and announced plans for a new class of non-voting stock on October 21, 2026, escalating its already enormous bet on artificial intelligence. Capital expenditures will be $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026, the company said during its quarterly earnings report, raising the bottom end of the range from $130 billion. The ceiling did not move — but the floor rose by $5 billion.

The money is going toward AI infrastructure: the chips and data centers needed to train large models, and the development of Muse, Meta's consumer AI agent. The quarterly results gave Meta some cover for the bigger budget. Third-quarter 2026 revenue came in at $64.60 billion, up 26% and ahead of the $63.37 billion Wall Street had expected, with diluted earnings per share of $3.83 after a $9.89 billion legal charge. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said: “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board.”

A new share class with no say

The new class of publicly listed Class C common stock carries no voting rights. Existing holders of Class A and Class B shares will receive a one-time dividend of one Class C share for every share they own, effective January 19, 2027 — in effect a two-for-one stock split. The stock will be used for capital fundraising, employee compensation and potential acquisitions, and the company said it could raise hundreds of billions of dollars over several years. Crucially, it lets Meta raise equity without diluting voting power: Zuckerberg holds around 61% of Meta's voting rights despite owning a smaller slice of its economic value.

Investors were not reassured. Meta shares fell more than 7% on Thursday, October 22, and the cost of insuring the company's debt against default hit an all-time high, Channel NewsAsia reported — the latest sign that fears over the cost of the AI race are spreading to credit markets. The selloff came despite better-than-expected results and strong fourth-quarter guidance, highlighting growing investor unease over AI spending that is pushing historically cash-rich tech companies toward debt.

The bigger question

Meta is not alone in spending at this scale, and that is precisely what worries markets: borrowing to fund data centers leaves AI companies exposed if demand cools, while chips depreciate within five or six years and force another round of spending. Meta's answer is that its core advertising business is strong enough to carry the bet. The market's answer, at least this week, was a selloff — and a reminder that even a revenue beat cannot always outrun a $145 billion spending plan.

articles.title: OpenAI Nears a $30 Billion Round at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation, Reports Say
articles.description: Reports say OpenAI is close to finalizing up to $30 billion in new funding led by Coatue and UAE investors — a deal that would make it the most valuable private company ever, if it closes on those terms.
articles.sources: TechCrunch, CNBC via TechCrunch, Business Times, Bloomberg via Business Times
articles.body:
OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding rather than plowing ahead with an initial public offering. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in the United Arab Emirates, sources told CNBC, as reported by TechCrunch on October 22, 2026. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change — and OpenAI declined to comment.

The figure is striking even by OpenAI's standards, and it is already lower than an earlier report. Bloomberg reported a month earlier that the lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. The Business Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported on October 23 that the value discussed had shifted down by $150 billion to $1.25 trillion, with investor commitments expected to be finalized by the end of the following week. Coatue Management is in talks to co-lead, and OpenAI has also been in talks with multiple UAE investment funds, among other firms including BlackRock, Bloomberg previously reported.

Why the UAE piece matters

The UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, CNBC reported — a detail that matters because so much of the company's spending goes toward chips and data centers. OpenAI's last completed round, in March 2026, brought in $122 billion in committed capital at an $852 billion post-money valuation, and the company filed confidential paperwork for an IPO in June. A completed round at the newly reported valuation would put OpenAI above the $1 trillion threshold and potentially establish it as the most valuable private company ever.

The timing is notable. Technology stocks fell in the same week after mixed quarterly earnings from Meta and Tesla fueled investor concerns that massive AI spending has gone too far, and rival Anthropic is reportedly preparing its own public debut — with CNBC reporting it is seeking a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation. OpenAI has pushed back its IPO plans until 2027, citing its focus on AI safety efforts, according to Bloomberg.

What to watch

Until commitments are signed, the $1.25 trillion figure remains a reported target, not a done deal. If it closes, it resets expectations for OpenAI's eventual public listing and signals that, even in a jittery market for AI stocks, the largest private investors are still willing to write the largest checks. If terms slip again, it will be read just as closely — as a measure of how much appetite remains for AI at any price.

articles.title: Rivian Buys UK Startup Third Dimension to Build Its Robotaxi Simulator
articles.description: Rivian has acquired Third Dimension AI, whose platform turns real-world footage into controllable 3D worlds, to accelerate driver assistance and its planned robotaxis for Uber.
articles.sources: Rivian announcement via Stockhouse, TechCrunch via Malakye, NewsBytes
articles.body:
Rivian Automotive announced on October 22, 2026, that it has acquired Third Dimension AI, Inc., a pioneer in AI-powered 3D spatial generation. The strategic transaction will accelerate synthetic data generation and full-world simulation for Rivian's driver assistance and self-driving systems. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.

Third Dimension AI, founded in 2024 by Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokolski, has developed a simulation platform that transforms real-world data into high-fidelity, controllable 3D environments, enabling complex driving scenarios to be recreated and varied at scale. Its 15-person team, mostly based in the United Kingdom, will join Rivian's Autonomy research and engineering teams. By bringing the team and platform in-house, Rivian said it will further expand its physical and virtual data flywheel.

Why simulation matters

“Simulation is central to how we train and validate our autonomous driving systems,” said James Philbin, Rivian's senior vice president of Autonomy and AI. “Third Dimension's team has built impressive technology that turns real-world data into detailed 3D environments. This allows us to recreate challenging driving situations, vary the conditions, and improve how our systems respond. Their technology and expertise will strengthen and accelerate autonomy across our consumer and robotaxi roadmaps.”

The logic is straightforward: autonomous vehicles need to learn how to handle rare or dangerous situations, but some of those situations may not occur often enough during normal road testing. Simulation lets Rivian recreate these edge cases repeatedly and safely. Philbin said Rivian receives more than 400,000 data sequences daily from customer vehicles whose owners have allowed data transmission from external cameras, and the acquisition is aimed at closing the gap between virtual worlds and actual roads.

The robotaxi angle

The deal supports Rivian's robotaxi plans with Uber, with a launch targeted for 2028, according to TechCrunch's reporting, as well as hands-free surface-street driving software targeted for release by the end of the year. Third Dimension co-founder and CEO Tolga Kart said: “Joining Rivian allows us to deploy our simulation technology at scale, accelerating both the generation of data needed to train autonomous systems and the validation needed to deploy them safely and reliably.” In a race where testing speed is everything, Rivian just bought itself a faster way to practice.

The acquisition lands alongside other autonomy milestones for Rivian. Self Drive News noted the company's Autonomy Early Access Program for point-to-point driving, launched on October 20, 2026, and its longer-term Level 4 autonomy roadmap. Together, the moves sketch a strategy that leans less on any single breakthrough and more on compounding advantages: real-world data from customer vehicles, synthetic data from simulation, and a validation loop that ties the two together. For a company competing with far larger rivals in self-driving, that flywheel — physical and virtual data feeding each other — is the bet the Third Dimension deal is designed to accelerate.
